source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: Replication of 10 claims comparing SBFL and mutation-based techniques. On artificial faults (mutants) 7 of 10 claims held as significant, but only 3 had non-negligible effect size.
numbers: 2995 artificial faults in 6 Java programs; 7 techniques. Overall 70% of earlier pairwise comparisons confirmed, 30% refuted.
limits: Artificial faults only. Re-implemented all techniques in one framework, which removes implementation differences.
agent_relevance: Rankings of scoring formulas learned on seeded or synthetic faults are weak evidence for real faults. Test any ranker on real faults.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: On real faults the artificial-fault ranking of techniques did not carry over. Every previous result was refuted or was statistically and practically insignificant. Ochiai beat Metallaxis on real faults, the reverse of the mutant result.
numbers: 310 real Defects4J faults from the same 6 programs. 40% of earlier results reversed, 60% insignificant.
quote: Artificial faults are not useful for predicting which fault localization techniques perform best on real faults.
limits: Java, Defects4J, single and multi-statement faults with a stated tie-handling rule.
agent_relevance: Do not tune the S5 ranker on injected bugs. Seeded-fault success can flip on real program attempts.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: The choice of SBFL formula barely matters on real faults. Formula explains at most 2% of non-defect variance in EXAM score. A Tukey test found all SBFL formula differences insignificant.
numbers: ANOVA over 395 real faults. Defect and debugging scenario dominate the variance. R2 = 0.65 for the SBFL model.
limits: Differences between formulas exist in the ANOVA (p<0.05) but are tiny. Applies to the 4 SBFL formulas studied (DStar, Ochiai, Barinel, Tarantula).
agent_relevance: Any reasonable formula works. Spend effort on the quality and number of tests, not on formula choice.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: A new hybrid (MCBFL-hybrid-avg) combining SBFL and mutation did better than any single technique, but gains were small in practice.
numbers: Top-5 / Top-10 on best-case scenario: hybrid 36% / 45%; DStar 30% / 39%; Metallaxis 29% / 39%. Average-case top-5: hybrid 23%, DStar 18%, Metallaxis 18%. Difference in EXAM not practically significant.
limits: Authors design the hybrid and test it on the same 395 faults they used to find it (selection risk). Best-case counts any one faulty statement.
agent_relevance: Even the best Java technique places the real fault in the top 5 in about a quarter to a third of cases. A rank list is a hint, not an answer.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and improving fault localization
finding: Ties and multi-line faults change scores. Authors treat tied statements as sharing the average rank and define best, worst and average-case debugging scenarios.
numbers: 76% of real bug fixes span multiple statements; 3 debugging scenarios in the protocol.
limits: Results depend on the scenario chosen. Reporting only best-case flatters every technique.
agent_relevance: When our agent ranks lines from pass/fail runs, count ties explicitly. Tied lines are the main failure of S5 coverage ranking on small programs.

source: Rezaalipour and Furia (2024) An Empirical Study of Fault Localization in Python Programs
finding: Conceptual replication of Zou et al.'s Java study on Python. SBFL was the most effective family, MBFL second. Predicate switching and stack-trace were less effective. Most Java findings carried over.
numbers: 135 faults in 13 BugsInPy projects; 7 techniques in 4 families; FauxPy tool. SBFL vs MBFL effect size -0.18 (weakly favours SBFL).
limits: Python only; statement-level default; dynamic typing and data science code change difficulty.
agent_relevance: SBFL results on Python programs are modest but follow the Java ordering.

source: Rezaalipour and Furia (2024) An Empirical Study of Fault Localization in Python Programs
finding: The three SBFL formulas Tarantula, Ochiai and DStar give nearly identical results. Per-bug rank correlations are very high and effect size differences vanish.
numbers: Rank correlation with DStar: Ochiai 0.99, Tarantula 0.94 (Fig. 8). Wilcoxon p about 0.056 to 0.093 between some formulas, with vanishing effect size.
limits: Same 135 bugs; statement-level.
agent_relevance: Formula choice is a non-issue; Ochiai is a fine default.

source: Rezaalipour and Furia (2024) An Empirical Study of Fault Localization in Python Programs
finding: Bugs in data-science projects are harder to localise than other categories. Mutation operators fit them poorly.
numbers: Mutability of data science bugs 0.7% vs 1.3% for other categories (reported in paper).
limits: Small project counts per category.
agent_relevance: Coverage ranking is weak where faults live in data or numeric values, not control flow. The agent should detect that case.

source: Rezaalipour and Furia (2024) An Empirical Study of Fault Localization in Python Programs
finding: Combining techniques raised effectiveness at a modest efficiency cost. Cross-benchmark comparison with Java found SBFL lower on Python, but the authors warn this comparison is not controlled.
numbers: SBFL put the fault in the top 10 in roughly a third of the 135 bugs (about 34 to 37%; the table was partly garbled in text extraction, so treat as approximate).
limits: Cross-language numbers compare different programs. Authors say such comparison is unlikely to give robust findings.
agent_relevance: Plan on SBFL alone placing the culprit in the top 10 for about one case in three on real Python bugs.

source: Rafi et al. (2025) SBEST: Spectrum-Based Fault Localization Without Fault-Triggering Tests
finding: SBFL needs a failing test. Only 3.33% of crash-report bugs had a failing test when the report was filed. Using stack traces as stand-in failing tests helped.
numbers: 60 crash bugs in Defects4J. SBEST raised MAP by 32.22% and MRR by 17.43% over baselines. Stack-trace ranking alone: 16 bugs top-1, 27 top-3, 34 top-5 (56.67% in top 5). Plain Ochiai found 2 in top 5 on the bugs where it could run.
limits: Small set of 60 bugs. Ochiai MAP/MRR without real failing tests were very low (e.g. 0.0693, 0.0836 in JacksonCore).
agent_relevance: Before running a ranker, check there is a real failing run. If there is only an error message, use it as the failing evidence (fits guardrail G2).

source: Callaghan and Fischer (2023) Improving Spectrum-Based Localization of Multiple Faults by Iterative Test Suite Reduction (FLITSR)
finding: SBFL accuracy decays as the number of faults grows, because faults mask each other. FLITSR repeatedly picks the top element and removes the tests it explains, then re-ranks.
numbers: 75000 synthetic variants of 15 projects with up to 32 faults, plus 326 real multi-fault Defects4J versions with up to 14 faults. Average wasted effort cut by 30% to 90% over best base metric; precision and recall gains generally 20% to 50% and about 30%.
limits: Synthetic faults inflate results; real faults gave larger gains at 1% inspected (about 62% vs 28% of faults found by FLITSR*). Gains vary by project; Time project shows no gain for the first fault.
agent_relevance: When several program attempts fail for different reasons, rank, address the top cause, drop the tests it explains, then re-rank. The program can run this loop by counting.

source: Callaghan and Fischer (2023) Improving Spectrum-Based Localization of Multiple Faults by Iterative Test Suite Reduction (FLITSR)
finding: FLITSR beat a learning-based localiser (GRACE) on real method-level faults, and improvements grow with the number of faults.
numbers: On synthetic data, AWE1 improvement over base metric rises from 3.2% (2 faults) to 42.5% (32 faults); AWE from 29.7% to 46.7%; P@5 from 30.3% to 60.2%.
limits: FLITSR (without star) did not reach significance on the median fault; only FLITSR* did.
agent_relevance: Mixed failure causes are the norm; single-fault ranking is the wrong default.

source: Naish et al.; Debroy and Wong; Xie et al. (2013) as summarised in de Souza et al. (2016) survey of spectrum-based fault localization
finding: Many ranking metrics are mathematically equivalent (e.g. Jaccard, Ochiai, Sorensen-Dice give the same ordering in the cited analysis). Xie et al. proved some metrics (O, Op, Wong1, Russel and Rao, Binary) rank at least as well as others for single-fault programs.
numbers: Xie et al. compared 30 metrics: six groups of equivalent metrics, seven with none.
limits: Proofs assume a single fault. Le et al. later found the theoretical result does not hold on well-studied programs; Ju et al. extended it to multiple faults.
agent_relevance: Theory favours a few simple metrics only under single-fault assumptions. Real programs break this, as Pearson 2017 also found.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? (as summarised in the 2016 survey)
finding: Human study with Tarantula. Developers did not follow the ranking order and used their own code knowledge. The rank of the true fault did not significantly change success.
numbers: Two programs, each with one fault. N not read; survey summary only.
limits: Known only through the 2016 survey (opened), not the original paper. Small, older study.
agent_relevance: A ranked list is not enough on its own. Explanation of why a line is suspicious matters (later LLM work adds this).

source: Xie et al. (2016) replication of Parnin and Orso, as summarised in the 2016 survey
finding: With students, SBFL helped only when the fault was ranked near the top, and often increased time spent.
numbers: 207 undergraduate students, 17 faults, programs up to 500 lines.
limits: Seen only through the survey. Students, small programs.
agent_relevance: If the true cause is not in the top few, the rank list can hurt. Cap trust at the top ranks.

source: Xia et al. (2016) follow-up study, as summarised in the 2016 survey
finding: Professional developers on real faults found SBFL improved both effectiveness and efficiency. Contrasts with the student result.
numbers: 36 professional developers, 16 real open-source faults.
limits: Seen only through the survey. Differences in population and fault realism may explain the disagreement.
agent_relevance: Evidence on usefulness is split; moderators are expertise and fault realism.

source: Perez and Abreu GZoltar user study and Kochhar et al. practitioner survey, as summarised in the 2016 survey
finding: With a visual SBFL tool all participants found the bug (about 7 minutes on average). Controls using Eclipse alone: only 35% found it in 30 minutes. A practitioner survey found people want the fault in the top 5.
numbers: GZoltar: 40 master's students, 20 per group, one fault. Kochhar: 386 practitioners.
limits: Single fault, one program, seen only via the survey. Pearson 2017 cites a related survey that says 98% need the fault in the top 10.
agent_relevance: Success target for S5 is the top 5 to 10 lines, not the single top line.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Large Language Models in Fault Localisation
finding: ChatGPT-4 at function level with the error log beat SBFL, MBFL and SmartFL on Top-1. At class level its accuracy fell sharply.
numbers: 46.9% higher Top-1 than SmartFL at function level; 49.9% lower than SmartFL at class level; removing the error log cut accuracy by 25.6% at Top-1.
limits: Defects4J plus a second benchmark; only small context works; ChatGPT versions change; possible data leakage.
agent_relevance: The LLM does well without coverage on short code and badly when context grows. Coverage evidence helps scale, so combine them.

source: Kang, An and Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: An LLM that navigates the repo by function calls beat Ochiai SBFL on method-level acc@1, but GPT-3.5 lagged SBFL at acc@3 and acc@5.
numbers: 798 bugs (Defects4J and BugsInPy). Acc@1 gain over Ochiai: +19.7% Defects4J, +166.7% BugsInPy (GPT-3.5), +233.3% BugsInPy (GPT-4). Time: 87.24 s per bug vs 112 s for SBFL (Zou et al.).
limits: SBFL is much worse on BugsInPy (known from Widyasari et al.). Needs the failing test coverage as input.
agent_relevance: The LLM wins at top-1; coverage ranking wins deeper in the list for weaker models. Use both.

source: Kang, An and Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: Repeating the LLM run and merging results helps a lot, and one GPT-4 run beat five merged GPT-3.5 runs. Agreement across runs gives a confidence estimate.
numbers: Merging up to 5 runs raised acc@k markedly on both benchmarks (Fig. 4).
limits: Repeated runs of one model are not independent (guardrail G4).
agent_relevance: Voting over repeated attempts helps ranking quality but is only a hint.

source: Qin et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based Fault Localization to Project-Level Context
finding: A multi-agent ChatGPT system using test failure info beat Ochiai at project level but not the best learning-based methods. It finds different bugs.
numbers: Defects4J 1.2.0, 395 bugs: 157 Top-1; 77 more than Ochiai, 3 fewer than FLUCCS, 19 fewer than DeepFLcov, 35 fewer than GRACE. Defects4J 2.0.0 (226 bugs): 46 more than Ochiai. Cost 0.074 dollars and 97 s per bug. 34 bugs found only by AgentFL.
limits: Closure project: LLMAO-with-Ochiai found 18 more. Top-3 and Top-5 below LLMAO-with-Ochiai.
agent_relevance: LLM and coverage ranking are complementary in which bugs they find.

source: Qin et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based Fault Localization to Project-Level Context
finding: Ablation: removing test-failure analysis or test-behaviour analysis hurts Top-1.
numbers: Top-1 of 395 bugs: without TestBehaviorAnalysis 148, without TestFailureAnalysis 125, without MethodDocEnhancement 133, full 157.
limits: One benchmark, one model (ChatGPT).
agent_relevance: Real test output is the most valuable input (fits G2).

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large Language Models for Test-Free Fault Localization (LLMAO)
finding: Fine-tuned LLM adapters locate buggy lines with no coverage at all, and improve with model size. The comparison is to learning-based baselines, not to SBFL formulas directly.
numbers: Top-1 gain over machine-learning FL baselines 2.3% to 54.4%; Top-5 gain 14.4% to 35.6%. Models of 350M, 6B and 16B parameters.
limits: Needs fine-tuning on a small bug corpus; baselines are other ML methods; possible train-test leakage in Defects4J.
agent_relevance: Test-free LLM ranking is a rival to S5; coverage is not strictly needed but adds a ground-truth signal.

source: Rafi et al. (2025) A Multi-Agent Approach to Fault Localization via Graph-Based Retrieval and Reflexion (LLM4FL)
finding: Multi-agent LLM using SBFL coverage chunks and a reflexion loop. Ochiai is the weakest baseline; removing parts of the pipeline lowers accuracy.
numbers: 675 Defects4J 2.0 bugs: LLM4FL 326 Top-1; Ochiai 121 (LLM4FL +169.4%), DeepFL 257, GRACE 298, DepGraph 359 (better), AutoFL 275. Ablation Top-1: without code navigation 273, without division 251, without reflexion 290 (vs 327).
limits: DepGraph still beat it. Reflexion gain is 6% to 11% without any external ground-truth feedback.
agent_relevance: Self-reflection helps only a little without external feedback (G2).

source: Widyasari et al. (2024) Demystifying Faulty Code with LLM (FuseFL)
finding: Giving the LLM SBFL suspiciousness scores helped, but test results helped more at Top-1. Combining scores, test results and a code description gave the best result.
numbers: Refactory student programs. FuseFL beats Ochiai by 68.4% at Top-1. Prompt table Top-1: baseline 150, SusScore 169, TestRes 187, FuseFL 197. SBFL-score prompt gave +44% over SBFL itself at Top-1. Of 77 cases SBFL missed in the top 3, only 8 found at Top-1. 22 of 30 sampled explanations were correct.
limits: Novice student programs; ChatGPT-3.5 only; small and may leak.
agent_relevance: SBFL scores in the prompt are a modest add-on; test outputs are stronger. Pass failing output first.

source: Yang et al. (2026) SemLoc: Executable and Verifiable Semantic Constraints
finding: Coverage collapse: on many real bugs failing and passing tests run the same lines, so every SBFL formula ties the faulty line. An LLM can write value checks that give a semantic violation spectrum instead.
numbers: 809 real bugs; 22.9% (185 programs) show coverage collapse. SBFL fails to rank the faulty line first in at least 83.8% of cases. On collapse programs: SemLoc 40.9% first, Ochiai 2.2%, Daikon 7.0%. Acc@1 81.4% vs 50.0% for an LLM seeing only the function.
limits: New dataset from the same authors; SemLoc is no better than an LLM given the same inputs (81.4% vs 82.0%).
agent_relevance: SBFL on wrong-value bugs fails by design. Fits our schema: LLM proposes checks, code runs them, code counts violations (G5).

source: Xu et al. (2025) Exploring the Potential and Limitations of LLMs for Novice Program Fault Localization
finding: Across 13 LLMs and three datasets, LLMs found far more faults than SBFL and MBFL, and traditional methods found few faults the LLMs missed.
numbers: Codeflaws: SBFL alone found 8 unique faults, MBFL 1 unique. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) best; non-reasoning GPT-4 needs careful prompts; accuracy drops with problem difficulty; over-reasoning hurts clarity.
limits: Novice-sized competition programs; exact Top-1 SBFL numbers were in garbled tables so not recorded.
agent_relevance: On small programs a strong LLM outranks coverage. SBFL adds mostly redundant coverage there.

source: Uddin et al. (2025) Studying the Impact of Early Test Termination Due to Assertion Failure on Code Coverage and SBFL
finding: A hidden cause of weak SBFL: a failing test stops at its first failed assertion so later code is never recorded as covered. Fixing this improves ranks.
numbers: 207 versions of 6 projects; 19.1% of failed tests terminate early; coverage improves in 55% of versions; Ochiai and Tarantula better by 15.1% and 10.7% in MFR.
limits: Java unit tests with multiple assertions.
agent_relevance: When the agent runs attempts, run to completion (collect all assertion failures) before ranking.

source: Gruber and Fraser (2023) Debugging Flaky Tests using SBFL
finding: Flaky tests break SBFL because coverage changes between runs. Using only the lines covered in every run narrows the fault to about 3.5% of the code base, 18.7% better than traditional SBFL (DStar).
numbers: 101 flaky tests from 48 Python projects; 80.3% of flaky tests show varying coverage; DStar, Ochiai and Op2 best.
limits: Works less well for order-dependent flakiness.
agent_relevance: Noisy or random program attempts need repeated runs before ranking.

source: Ribeiro et al. (2019) Evaluating data-flow coverage in SBFL
finding: Richer spectra can improve ranking: data-flow spectra put up to 50% more faults in the top 15 than line coverage, at higher cost.
numbers: 5 real programs with 468 to 4130 tests; overhead 353% for data-flow vs 102% for control-flow.
limits: Small number of programs.
agent_relevance: Choosing a better signal beats choosing a better formula (same message as Pearson 2017).
